strengths: Addresses a novel and practically important problem: no prior work has tackled training-free concept unlearning specifically for video diffusion models, and the paper clearly positions this gap relative to image-domain methods (UCE, RECE).

The proposed method is elegant and data-efficient, requiring only 5 safe/unsafe multimodal prompt pairs, and derives a clean closed-form weight update (Eq. 8) that can be permanently fused into the model with no added inference cost.

Technically sound derivation: the low-rank/cPCA subspace projection is well motivated (isolating the forget concept while excluding retain-set directions) and the algebra connecting the subspace correction to a closed-form weight update is rigorously shown in the appendix.

Reasonably thorough qualitative evaluation across five diverse harmful-content categories (nudity, gore, copyrights/trademarks, dangerous actions, public figures), with many additional examples in the appendix and full prompt lists for reproducibility.
Useful ablations on cPCA rank and the lambda suppression coefficient, showing sensible trends and providing practical guidance on hyperparameter choice.
Good identification and discussion of limitations (dual-use/misuse risk, adversarial reversibility of the vector, single-concept removal at a time).
weaknesses: No baseline comparisons whatsoever: despite extensively discussing UCE, RECE, Forget-Me-Not, MACE, etc. in related work, the paper never adapts or compares against any of them (even naive extensions) on the same benchmark, making it impossible to judge whether the proposed method's censorship/quality trade-off is actually better than simpler alternatives (e.g., prompt filtering, naive activation subtraction without low-rank projection, or a simple fine-tuning baseline).

The abstract and introduction claim the weight-editing approach is inherently more robust against adversarial bypass attempts than input/output filters, but no adversarial robustness experiments (e.g., prompt paraphrasing, jailbreak prompts, or embedding perturbations) are provided to support this central safety claim.

Quantitative improvements in Table 2 (MM-Notox) are very small (1.85%-5.31%), which is a weak signal for the claimed strong semantic decontamination, especially compared to the more dramatic drops reported in Table 1; the paper does not reconcile or analyze this discrepancy.

FVD values in Table 2 are reported only for the proposed method with no baseline or original-model FVD for direct comparison (only a loose reference to FVD vs. pure noise), making it hard to assess how much quality is actually preserved relative to alternatives.

Evaluation is conducted on a single backbone (OPEN-SORA); no experiments on other video diffusion architectures are provided to support generality claims implied by the 'first framework for video diffusion models' contribution.

Safety evaluation relies solely on a single automated GPT-4 frame-level judge with no human verification or inter-rater reliability check within this paper, and sample sizes per category are not reported.

The method requires white-box access to model weights, and the single-concept-at-a-time limitation is acknowledged but not addressed with any multi-concept composition experiment, which would be important for realistic deployment.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: unlearning/safety editing for video diffusion models, as opposed to only image diffusion models.

The method is training-free, requires only 5 prompt pairs per concept, and the closed-form weight-fusion derivation (absorbing the subspace projection into the FFN weights) is mathematically explicit and reproducible in principle.
Leveraging both text and image conditioning for concept extraction is a sensible design choice given the multimodal nature of modern video DiT backbones.
Reasonably broad qualitative coverage across five unsafe categories (nudity, gore, copyright/trademarks, dangerous actions, public figures) with many example prompts shown in the appendix.
Authors provide some ablations (cPCA rank, λ) and an explanation of which transformer blocks are most effective to edit.
weaknesses: No baselines whatsoever: despite extensive discussion of UCE and RECE as prior training-free unlearning methods, the paper does not adapt or compare against any existing method (even a naive adaptation to video cross-attention), making it impossible to judge whether the proposed low-rank refusal vector offers any real advantage over simpler alternatives (e.g., plain refusal-vector subtraction without cPCA, or applying UCE/RECE-style edits to the video model's text/image cross-attention).

Residual unsafe-content rates remain substantial after 'unlearning' (33% for Copyright/Trademarks, 13.4% for Pornography, 9.1% for Sequential Action Risk), which undercuts the abstract's claim of 'neutralizing' harmful content; the actual numbers suggest partial mitigation rather than robust removal, yet the framing throughout the paper is uniformly positive.

Apparent dimensional inconsistency in the covariance derivation: R is defined as H×N but Cr = R̄ᵀR̄ is stated to be in R^{H×H}, which is only correct if R̄ is N×H (or if Cr = R̄R̄ᵀ). This notational/mathematical error is never clarified, and combined with only N=5 pairs it is unclear how the ablation can meaningfully sweep rank k up to 12200, since a sample covariance from 5 points should have rank ≤4. This raises real concerns about the clarity and soundness of the core technical contribution.

No held-out / general-purpose video quality benchmark (e.g., VBench) is used to verify that edits do not degrade the model's broader generative capability beyond the specific unsafe prompts tested; FVD is only computed relative to the paper's own unsafe-video set and a trivial 'noise' sanity check, which is a weak proxy for quality preservation.

The paper explicitly claims improved robustness against 'adversarial bypass attempts' compared to input-output filters, but no adversarial/jailbreak evaluation is conducted to substantiate this central safety claim.

Reliance on a single automated GPT-4 frame-level evaluator for the primary safety metric, with no human validation specific to this paper's video outputs (only citing that the benchmark's own evaluator correlates with humans in a different context), and no reported sample sizes, variance, or multiple generation seeds for statistical reliability.

Limited novelty: the core techniques (refusal/steering vectors from Arditi et al., contrastive PCA from Abid et al.) are adopted largely as-is from prior work in different domains; the primary contribution is their combination and application to video diffusion models rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The method is demonstrated only for single-concept removal; the stated limitation that concepts must be removed one at a time, combined with no experiments on sequential or simultaneous multi-concept edits, limits practical significance for real-world deployment where many concepts would need to be suppressed simultaneously.
No comparison of computational/curation cost or effectiveness trade-offs against simply applying safety filters or prompt rewriting, which the paper dismisses early on without empirical comparison.

strengths: Addresses a novel and practically important problem: training-free concept unlearning specifically for video diffusion models, which the paper convincingly argues has not been addressed before (prior work like UCE/RECE targets image diffusion only).

The technical approach is well-motivated: extending 'refusal vector' steering to a permanent weight edit, and introducing contrastive PCA on the covariance difference between forget and retain sets to isolate a low-rank subspace for the target concept, reducing collateral damage to unrelated semantics.

Extremely data-efficient (only 5 safe/unsafe prompt pairs per concept) and training-free, with the correction absorbed into a closed-form weight update (Eq. 8) that adds no inference-time latency or memory overhead.
Novel use of multimodal (text + image) conditioning inputs for concept extraction, shown empirically to better preserve unrelated semantics than text-only extraction.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation across five distinct harmful categories (nudity, gore, copyright/trademarks, dangerous actions, public figures), using an established benchmark (T2VSafetyBench) plus FVD and an adapted MM-Notox metric, alongside ablations on cPCA rank and the λ suppression coefficient.

Good reproducibility effort: detailed derivations in the appendix (full closed-form update derivation), explicit statement of which layers are edited and why, extensive additional qualitative examples, and a stated commitment to release code.
weaknesses: No baseline comparisons: despite discussing UCE and RECE at length, the paper does not attempt to adapt or approximate these (or any other) methods as baselines for video unlearning, making it impossible to gauge how much the proposed low-rank refusal vector improves over simpler alternatives (e.g., a naive full-rank refusal vector without cPCA, which is actually available as an ablation but not framed as a baseline comparison against prior unlearning ideas).

Single backbone evaluation: all experiments are conducted only on OPEN-SORA; no evidence is provided that the method generalizes to other video diffusion architectures (e.g., CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo), which weakens the generality claims implied by the title and contributions.

Evaluation relies entirely on an automated GPT-4 frame-level classifier for safety and on FVD/MM-Notox for quality; no human study or user evaluation is conducted to corroborate perceptual quality or the subtlety of the reported collateral changes (e.g., whether unrelated content truly remains intact beyond the cherry-picked qualitative examples).

The claimed 'single scalar hyperparameter λ' controllability is somewhat overstated, since the method also depends on the cPCA rank k, the contrastive weighting α, and the specific choice/size of the retain set R, all of which appear to require per-category or per-model tuning (e.g., the layer selection 17-19 was found via manual sweep) without a principled or automatic selection procedure.

The robustness-to-adversarial-bypass claim is asserted but not empirically tested (e.g., no red-teaming, adversarial prompt search, or jailbreak-style evaluation), and the paper's own limitations section admits the refusal direction could be inverted to reintroduce or even implant harmful concepts, undercutting the central 'more robust against adversarial bypass' selling point.

FVD and MM-Notox results are reported without reference points from any competing unlearning method or ablated variant (e.g., full-rank vs. low-rank editing), making it hard to judge whether the observed quality preservation is meaningfully better than naive alternatives.

The method unlearns only one concept at a time (acknowledged as a limitation), which may limit practical deployment where multiple harmful categories must be suppressed simultaneously, and the paper does not explore whether multiple refusal vectors can be composed without interference.

Ablation curves (e.g., censorship score vs. cPCA rank) appear to be based on single runs without variance/error bars, so it is unclear whether the observed non-monotonic trend (optimum at k=100) is a robust or noisy artifact.

strengths: Addresses a clear and underexplored gap: training-free, closed-form weight-update unlearning specifically for video diffusion models, as opposed to filtering (SAFREE) or costly fine-tuning (NullSCE) approaches used previously in the video domain.

Clean and rigorous mathematical derivation showing the subspace-aware refusal correction can be exactly absorbed into a linear layer's weights (Appendix B), yielding a truly training-free, zero-inference-overhead update.

Extensive experimental validation across two backbones (Open-Sora, ZeroScopeT2V) and two benchmarks (T2VSafetyBench, SafeSora), using three complementary metrics (censorship rate, FVD, MM-Notox) plus an additional motion-consistency metric (FVMD) in the appendix.

Thorough ablation studies covering cPCA rank, suppression strength λ, safe/unsafe prompt-pair similarity, neutral-set resampling stability, and cPCA vs. plain PCA/refusal-only, which strengthen confidence in the method's robustness to hyperparameter choices.
Very data- and compute-efficient: only 5 prompt pairs and negligible compute (~$1 estimated) compared to full training or fine-tuning, which is a practically appealing property for deployment.

Additional appendix experiments (mass/multi-concept erasure, adaptation of UCE to video as an extra baseline, adversarial prompting robustness, neutral concept sensitivity) demonstrate diligence in stress-testing the method beyond the main results.
Extensive and diverse qualitative results across five safety categories with clear before/after comparisons support the quantitative claims.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons are not symmetric/unified: NullSCE is only compared on Open-Sora/T2VSafetyBench and SAFREE only on ZeroScopeT2V/SafeSora, so there is no single benchmark where all methods (including UCE) are compared head-to-head under identical conditions, making relative ranking claims (e.g., 'outperforms NullSCE by X%') harder to fully trust.

FVD results are mixed rather than uniformly preserved: several categories (e.g., Violence, Sexual, Animal Abuse in Table 2; Public Figures in Table 1) show FVD increases after unlearning, partially undercutting the claim that video quality is fully preserved.

Key hyperparameters (target layers 17-18, rank k, λ=1) appear to be manually tuned per architecture/category, and it is unclear how well this generalizes to new architectures or a larger set of unseen concepts without repeating this tuning process.

The theoretical justification for linear 'refusal directions' existing cleanly in video diffusion spatio-temporal activations is largely inherited from LLM/image literature; the paper does not provide strong new theoretical grounding specific to the video setting beyond empirical validation.

Multi-concept (mass) erasure results show noticeable degradation in quality and increasing entanglement as more refusal vectors are combined (e.g., FVD spikes with 5 vectors), raising scalability concerns for realistic deployment scenarios requiring simultaneous removal of many unsafe concepts.

The core technical contribution is largely a combination/adaptation of existing techniques (LLM refusal vectors, contrastive PCA, UCE/RECE-style closed-form edits) to a new modality, which, while useful, limits the conceptual novelty relative to prior work.

Reliance on a GPT-4o automated judge for censorship rate as the primary safety metric, with only benchmark-level (not paper-specific) validation against human judgment, leaves some uncertainty about evaluation fidelity for this specific method's outputs.

Ethical/legal considerations around the 'Public Figures' unlearning use case (e.g., identity rights, potential biases in which figures/faces are more easily suppressed) are demonstrated qualitatively but not discussed in depth.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: concept unlearning for text-to-video diffusion models, where existing solutions (filtering, fine-tuning) are either reversible/bypassable or costly.
The closed-form derivation showing how the subspace-aware projection can be folded into layer weights (Section 3.2, Appendix B) is mathematically careful and clearly presented.

Extensive ablation studies are provided: cPCA rank, suppression strength λ, number/similarity of prompt pairs, neutral-set resampling, and PCA vs cPCA comparison, which do lend some support to the robustness of hyperparameter choices.

Appendix contains additional experiments (UCE adaptation baseline, mass/multi-concept erasure, adversarial prompting robustness, compute/cost comparison) that attempt to contextualize the contribution more broadly.
The method is computationally cheap (no retraining, ~5 prompt pairs, negligible inference overhead), which is an appealing practical property if the core claims hold up.
weaknesses: Core comparisons are not apples-to-apples: NullSCE is only compared against on Open-Sora/T2VSafetyBench and SAFREE only against ZeroScope/SafeSora. There is no experiment comparing all methods on the same backbone/benchmark, making the headline 'outperforms SOTA' claims hard to verify and seemingly cherry-picked to favorable pairings.

The refusal vector is estimated from only 5 hand-crafted safe/unsafe prompt pairs per concept; while an ablation shows adding more pairs doesn't help, this says little about generalization beyond the narrow prompt templates used (see Appendix E, which shows fairly formulaic, similar-structure prompts), raising concerns about overfitting to superficial lexical cues (e.g., the word 'naked') rather than a genuine semantic direction.

Sole reliance on a GPT-4o binary judge for the primary safety metric (censorship rate) without any human evaluation specific to this paper's generations is a significant limitation; automated VLM judges are known to have systematic biases and blind spots, especially for borderline/implicit unsafe content.

FVD, the chosen fidelity metric, actually increases (gets worse) for the ZeroScope/SafeSora experiments in every category (Table 2) and in several multi-vector/mass-erasure settings, which is somewhat in tension with the repeated claim that 'video quality is not degraded.'

The paper repeatedly frames the edit as 'permanent' and 'irreversible,' directly referencing the risk of concept resurgence in the related-work discussion, yet never tests whether the proposed weight edit is actually robust to resurgence (e.g., via light fine-tuning or further prompting), leaving this central safety claim unverified.

Hyperparameters such as the target layers (17–18) and rank k are selected via per-model, seemingly manual search with limited justification for how these would transfer to new/larger architectures (e.g., CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo, Sora-like commercial models), undermining claims of general applicability beyond the two relatively dated/small models tested.

Mass-erasure results (Appendix C.3) show clear degradation (sharp FVD increase, inconsistent censorship gains) once more than ~4 concepts are composed, suggesting the method may not scale to realistic deployment scenarios requiring removal of many concepts simultaneously.

Several qualitative 'successes' (e.g., adding a window railing for 'sequential action risk', described in Fig. 2) look more like prompt-level content substitution/steering than a disentangled concept-removal operation, raising questions about whether the method is cleanly isolating a 'concept direction' versus just suppressing salient attention activations in a somewhat ad hoc way.

The adversarial robustness evaluation (Appendix H) is very narrow (one attack type, 100 prompts from a single category), insufficient to support any strong claim of robustness against adaptive/jailbreak attacks, which is an important threat model for an 'open-weight safety' framing.

The improvement in MM-Notox and censorship numbers in the main tables, while positive, are often modest in several categories (e.g., Public Figures 10%→2%, Sexual on SafeSora 51.5%→9.1% vs. baseline for SAFREE only 18.2%, but these are all single-run numbers without variance/confidence intervals, so the statistical reliability of reported gains is unclear).

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: prior video-safety approaches are either inference-time filtering (SAFREE, VideoEraser) or costly fine-tuning (NullSCE); this is the first training-free, closed-form weight-update method for concept unlearning in video diffusion models.

The technical derivation is rigorous and self-contained: the refusal-vector projection is formally shown to be exactly absorbable into a linear layer's weights (Appendix B gives a full derivation with orthogonality/isometry arguments), making the method truly training-free and inference-cost-free.

The contrastive low-rank PCA (cPCA) refinement is well motivated (avoiding entanglement between unsafe and safe/neutral directions) and empirically validated via a clean ablation ladder (refusal-only → +PCA → +cPCA, Table 5) showing monotonic improvement.

Evaluation spans two distinct model architectures (Open-Sora DiT, ZeroScopeT2V/ModelScope) and two established benchmarks (T2VSafetyBench, SafeSora), using three complementary metrics (censorship rate, FVD, MM-Notox) rather than a single proxy for safety.

Extensive appendix experiments substantially strengthen the paper: FVMD for temporal coherence, compute/data-efficiency comparison against full training and fine-tuning, multi-concept/mass erasure analysis, an adapted UCE baseline for T2V with hyperparameter sweep, neutral-set and rank/lambda sensitivity studies, and a targeted adversarial-prompt robustness test.

Qualitative results across 5 diverse unsafe categories (pornography, gore, copyright, public figures, sequential action risk) are extensive and visually convincing, with quality apparently preserved in unrelated regions of the scene.

Practical efficiency: needs only 5 paired prompts and negligible compute (~$1, 10 forward passes) versus thousands of GPU-hours for fine-tuning, which is a meaningful deployment advantage for open-weight model sanitization.
weaknesses: The head-to-head comparisons are not fully crossed: NullSCE is only compared on Open-Sora/T2VSafetyBench and SAFREE only on ZeroScope/SafeSora, so there is no single setting where all three methods (ours, filtering, fine-tuning) are compared directly against each other.

Only two, relatively smaller/older video backbones are tested (Open-Sora, ZeroScope); no experiments on larger contemporary models mentioned in related work (e.g., CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo), which limits confidence that the method scales to state-of-the-art architectures.

FVD does not uniformly improve or stay flat after intervention (e.g., several categories in Table 2 show FVD increasing post-edit), so the 'quality preserved' claim is only approximately supported and not statistically tested for significance given the modest per-category sample sizes.

The safety/censorship metric relies solely on a single automatic GPT-4o judge; no independent human evaluation is reported in this paper to corroborate the automated scores for the specific settings tested (only a citation to prior validation in the benchmark paper).

Choice of layer (17–18) is stated as empirically found best but the systematic layer-sweep supporting this claim is not shown in the main text or appendix, limiting reproducibility/verifiability of this key hyperparameter.

The mass-erasure experiment shows that combining more than ~4 refusal vectors causes a marked FVD/quality degradation, raising open questions about scalability to realistic deployment scenarios needing many simultaneous concept removals.

Adversarial robustness evaluation is limited to a single attack type on a small 100-prompt subset within one category (pornography), which is a fairly narrow test of the permanence claims made for the method.

Ethical implications of erasing public figures' likeness (a legally/ethically distinct category from nudity/violence/copyright) are not discussed despite being included as a benchmark category and showcased extensively in qualitative results.
